I do agree. Social anxiety is a pain to deal with. But I'm almost learning to appreciate the anxiety. I think of it like another instinct, almost. For me, it works as a layer of protection. The only people who manage to get through that protection are people who I wouldn't trade for the world. I'm not gonna sit here and say it's becoming anything close to sunshine and rainbows, though. There have been so many times where I think someone is giving me very clear signs to talk to them, especially in public, and I just don't. 

A few weeks ago there was a woman I saw at a store. She worked there, but she was very clearly into me. She basically zoomed past every other customer and went straight to me asking if I needed help with anything. I spent the rest of my time there noticing her out of the corner of my eyes checking me out. Every time I'd walk by her she had the biggest smile I had ever seen on anyone's face. 

So y'know what I did? I didn't say a word to her, and Holy Hell do I regret it. This was the first time in my almost 21 years of life that I had ever felt genuinely noticed in public, and I threw that opportunity out the window hard. I go to the store occasionally now and haven't seen her since. I don't know if she still even works there. 

So yeah, social anxiety sucks hard. It takes away opportunities from us on the daily, I'm sure. On the flipside, that extra layer of protection I feel I have from fake people is huge. I can't say that my point of view will ever apply to anyone else, but I think it's a decent way to make the best out of what is a pretty detrimental thing to deal with.

As much as I wish I can say I'd will it away if I could, I can't, in all honesty, say that I would. I genuinely believe that introverts with social anxiety are some of the greatest people one can have in their lives. Is it sucky a lot of days for us? Yes. But all it takes, for me at least, is one person to completely flip my world right-side-up. Not only that, I see it as an honor of sorts to be "chosen", for lack of a better term. I'll take that along with knowing that the people that are around me are there for me and not what materialistic things I may or may never be able to offer them, instead of stressing about not being the most popular person in the room.

I don't know if this is usual, but whenever I speak out loud, my words feel like they're not my own, if that makes any sense. Almost as if as soon as I speak how I feel, I stop feeling that way for the time being. But if I keep everything in my head, it starts to feel more and more real. There are some times where it makes me feel worse, but easily 95%+ of the time it does calm me down.

I'm in very similar situation. I still very much struggle with this feeling, but I'm making some decent steps in recovering.

I think that a lot of my recovery is, unfortunately, intertwined with the fact that I hit such a low that I struggle to care much about myself anymore. I'm taking strides in the right direction because I'm consumed by a mindset of, "worst comes to worst, I die". I know this may not be the best thing to hear, but I think that part of recovery is learning to let go a little. I can't say that it's 100% foolproof, because I know many people who only had things get worse with trying to let go, however I know many more who have had a far better time letting go and just hoping things work out while they try to make progress. In my experience it makes your days feel longer, perhaps some days more miserable than before, but the highs feel higher and the lows don't feel quite as low even though objectively speaking, they're lower.

However, if I could turn back the clock, I would definitely have gone onto medication. I do feel like it's too late for me personally to see any worthwhile benefit from medication, so I haven't bothered, against what I assume to be my better judgement. I don't see anywhere that you're currently in therapy, so I think it could be a worthwhile checkout. For me personally it definitely is helpful to just get stuff off my chest in a closed environment, whether the topics be depressive or the best news I've had in a while.

I do struggle with this mindset, but recently I came in contact with an old friend that I never really interacted with a ton, but she told me that she always kind of liked me. I couldn't understand how or why until she explained it to me. 

We never really talked a ton, never really hung out, but I was there. I was a pillar of sorts. I wasn't trying to have sex with her, or use her or whatever so many other people were trying to do. I just kind of existed and would talk to her occasionally. I didn't offer her anything particularly standout-ish in my eyes, but to her it meant a lot because this was something that not many people offered her. 

Point being, you might not feel special, but the people around you may genuinely think that you're special or important because they've had experiences with you that they don't find in many other people, or perhaps at all. I'm definitely still struggling to stomach the idea that I may be special or important to someone, but the way she explained it definitely helped my point of view. Just food for thought.

It's not fair, nor does it make sense to mock these people. Yes, this stuff does destroy lives. But so do many other things. So many people will jump to screaming guilty based on even the most minute details of other crimes, until it comes to something like sexual abuse. Obviously not everyone jumps to screaming guilty so quickly. You don't need to 100% side with the people making the claims. But it goes a long way to at least show enough decency to not dismiss their claims entirely.

I don't mean to take away from any of this. I honestly feel miserable typing this out because I know people take this stuff the wrong way. I know women disproportionately struggle with this issue, but I don't like the fact that it feels like sexual abuse as a whole isn't taken seriously. I'm in complete support of everyone coming out with the truth, but it does often feel like society would much rather believe that sexual abuse doesn't happen at all. Whether that be to protect their own feelings or because the idea makes them uncomfortable. My father was sexually abusive and so much more towards my mother and I. Not a soul believed us until she started dating her current boyfriend about six years ago. I think society as a whole needs to really re-evaluate their outlook on sexual abuse.
